newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India, Pakistan cotton likely to remain subdued.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan cotton likely to remain subdued.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to remain depressed in India and Pakistan in the next few days, dealers in the two countries said on Thursday.
In India, cotton prices are likely to remain subdued as supplies from the 1996/97 crop (Oct/Sept) pick up considerably, dealers in Bombay said.
"Fresh demand from cotton mills petered out under pressure from new crop arrivals, especially in the north," said a trader.
He said daily supplies of cotton from India's Punjab state, which remained low because of last week's local elections, had begun picking up.
In the week to Thursday, Bengal-deshi fell 25 rupees to 750/800 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginned 10/15 rupees to 1,375/1,610 per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) dropped 400/500 rupees to 11,000/11,300 per candy (355.56 kg) and Sankar-4 (long staple) fell 500 to 16,000/18,000 rupees per candy.
Market sentiment remained depressed as an expected rise in the export quota for the 1996/97 season did not materialise, dealers said.
Recently, the Indian government authorised fresh exports of 165,000 bales (170 kg) of cotton, making 1.22 million bales for the 1996/97 season.
Traders said a meeting of the Cotton Advisory Board (CAB) in India's federal textiles ministry had been convened for February 24 to assess cotton demand and supply for 1996/97.
CAB had earlier estimated the 1996/97 crop at 15.50 million bales against 16 million the previous year.

In Pakistan, prices are likely to fall as ginners, who are holding more than 1.8 million 375-lb bales of stocks on expectations of higher prices, cannot hold any longer, dealer Amir Merchant in Karachi said.
"Ginners have to offload the unsold stocks in the market and at that time prices will ease," he said.
The textile sector is buying a few lots of bales but exporters are on the sidelines waiting for high domestic prices to fall to 2,000 rupees per maund, he said.
He said exports were not profitable at current prices but "the situation would clear by the end of February."
Merchant said there was a feeling in the market that exports could start from the third week of March if prices fell to 2,000 rupees per maund.
A Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association executive said ginners were holding 1.807 million bales of unsold stocks as at February 6 compared to 1.537 million a year ago.

Pakistan's cotton production reached 8.167 million bales by February 6 compared to 9.250 million in the year-ago period. The textile sector had bought 6.355 million bales compared to 6.703 million a year ago and private exporters 3,900 bales compared to 1.009 million.

A spokesman for the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said exporters had registered only 21,503 bales for exports with the state-run Export Promotion Bureau by February 6 compared to 1.929 million in the year-ago period.
Government officials estimate ex-gin production will be nine million bales, enough for spinning industry consumption estimated at 8.5 to 9.0 million bales.
In the Pakistani kerb market, NIAB-78 variety ranged between 2,300 and 2,325 rupees per maund.
